summary: Discusses how privacy threats apply to IPv6 over various link layers and gives protocol designers advice on addressing them in adaptation-layer specifications. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: IPv6 addresses can reveal which device is connecting and may let observers follow it across networks. This RFC advises protocol designers to make interface identifiers difficult to guess and able to change.

questions: how many bits of entropy does an ipv6 interface identifier need
why are short addresses bad for ipv6 privacy
subtitle: Privacy guidance for IPv6 interface identifiers on constrained and low-power links.

tldr.problem: An IPv6 interface identifier with too little entropy for the lifetime of a link can make devices easier to track, identify, or find by scanning.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC relates address-scanning risk to the number of devices and the link lifetime, then considers IEEE identifiers and short link-layer addresses.
tldr.outcome: It recommends that adaptation-layer specifications explain scan protection, provide sufficient identifier entropy, and allow addresses to change over time and across networks.

facts.label: Entropy example for a long-lived link

today: RFC 8065 is an Informational document published in February 2017. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Privacy Risks from IPv6 Interface Identifiers
sections.content:
An interface identifier (IID) with too little entropy for the lifetime of a link can expose users to several privacy risks. A stable IID can link activity over time or reveal movement when used with different network prefixes. It can also help an observer identify a device type or scan for addresses.

The RFC notes that link-local addresses can also leak through higher-layer protocols. It points to existing recommendations for opaque and temporary IPv6 addresses, while focusing on guidance for adaptation-layer specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: A predictable interface identifier can help an observer recognize a device or follow it between networks. Changing identifiers can reduce those privacy risks.

sections.title: How Much Entropy Address Scanning Needs
sections.content:
The RFC identifies scanning of routable addresses as the privacy threat that needs the most entropy. Where devices do not answer unsolicited traffic, a scanner may rely on the absence of an ICMP unreachable message. The RFC uses a typical limit of two such messages per second in its example.

Its rule of thumb is to add the base-two logarithm of the number of devices per link to the base-two logarithm of the link lifetime in seconds, then add two. For the example of at most 2^16 devices and a link lifetime of 8 years (2^28 seconds), the RFC says at least 46 bits of entropy are needed for a scan to take longer than the link lifetime to have a 50% chance of a hit. It says 59 or more bits are needed when the address must also resist spoofing.
sections.plainLanguage: Long-lived links and links with many devices need more unpredictable address bits. The RFC's example requires at least 46 bits for privacy against scanning and 59 or more bits when spoofing protection is also needed.

sections.title: IEEE Identifiers and Short Addresses
sections.content:
Some link technologies use IEEE identifiers or arbitrary 64-bit identifiers. Using these can simplify stateless header compression, but an identifier may not provide enough entropy for a routable IPv6 address. Changing or randomizing link-layer addresses can reduce some privacy risks.

A short link-layer address padded with fixed bits does not provide enough entropy unless the link is very short-lived. The RFC gives a possible alternative: combine a short address with a shared secret using a one-way hash to spread the result across the interface-identifier space.
sections.plainLanguage: A fixed hardware identifier may be too predictable, and padding a short address with fixed bits does not make it private. A specification can instead use randomized addresses or combine a short address with a shared secret.

sections.title: Recommendations for Adaptation-Layer Specifications
sections.content:
The RFC recommends that specifications explain how they mitigate address scans and show that the available entropy matches the maximum link lifetime. They should define a way to include sufficient entropy in the IID, such as allowing randomized link-layer addresses where supported.

Specifications should avoid padding short addresses with fixed bits except under the conditions described in the RFC. They should allow addresses to change over time to reduce correlation, and allow IIDs to vary per network when devices can roam.
sections.plainLanguage: Specifications should explain how their addresses resist scanning for the expected link lifetime. They should also allow addresses to change over time and when a device joins a different network.
